label: Stop Prolonged Beyond Its Original Purpose

trigger.description: Ask whenever there was a traffic or investigative stop, to determine whether it was extended beyond the time reasonably required for its original purpose.

non_gating_questions.q_stop_type: Used only to route which vehicle-stop-timeline questions get asked at all (decision-tree concern) — not part of this issue's match condition.

review_conditions.display_note: It's unclear whether the officer developed independent reasonable suspicion during the original-purpose tasks. If it turns out suspicion did arise then, the extension may be independently justified and this issue could be weaker than presented — confirm the timeline (dispatch log, body-cam) before relying on this issue as written.

segments.text: A traffic stop becomes unlawful if it is prolonged beyond the time reasonably required to complete the mission of the stop. Rodriguez v. United States, 575 U.S. 348 (2015). Authority for the seizure ends when tasks tied to the traffic infraction are, or reasonably should have been, completed, and an officer may not extend an otherwise-completed stop, even briefly, to conduct a dog sniff or other unrelated investigation absent independent reasonable suspicion. Illinois v. Caballes, 543 U.S. 405 (2005), permits a dog sniff only if it does not add time to the stop. Where an officer develops reasonable, articulable suspicion of additional criminal activity during the stop's original mission, a brief extension to investigate that suspicion may be justified; the burden is on the government to establish that suspicion arose before, not after, the original mission concluded.

authorities.name: Rodriguez v. United States
propositions: stop unlawful once prolonged beyond original mission

authorities.name: Illinois v. Caballes
propositions: dog sniff permissible only if it adds no time to the stop

segments.text: Alaska has adopted this same rule for traffic stops conducted by Alaska law enforcement: a stop is unlawfully extended once the officer has, or reasonably should have, completed the tasks tied to the stop's original purpose, and any further extension without independent reasonable suspicion violates the Fourth Amendment. Simmons v. State, 435 P.3d 975 (Alaska App. 2018) (applying Rodriguez v. United States to hold that a traffic stop was unlawfully prolonged).

authorities.name: Simmons v. State
propositions: Alaska Court of Appeals applies Rodriguez's prohibition on prolonging a traffic stop beyond its original purpose

practice_notes: Rodriguez rejects a bright-line minimum delay — even a short, unjustified extension can violate the Fourth Amendment, so don't discount this issue just because the added time was brief.
Get the dispatch log and any body-cam/dash-cam timestamps in discovery early — this issue lives and dies on minute-by-minute sequencing.
Pin down the officer's own testimony on when each original-purpose task was completed; officers sometimes pad task completion time in reports to avoid a Rodriguez problem.
If a K-9 unit was called before the original tasks were done, that timing itself can be favorable — it suggests intent to prolong regardless of what happened later.
